title: Credibility assessment: Demeanor fails without proven replacement
desc: Challenges traditional lie detection using evidence against demeanor and expert advantage, while separating reliability, performance and admissibility.

kps.k: The cluster challenges traditional credibility assessment without establishing that technological lie detection offers a superior replacement.
kps.d: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice questions the presumed deception-detection advantage of face-to-face confrontation. Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward contrasts praise for cross-examination with the scientific literature on psychometric deception detection. Both question the evidential basis for established practices, but the latter's bibliographic comparison does not demonstrate comparative accuracy.

kps.k: The strongest reported evidence concerns unreliable demeanor cues and the absence of an expert advantage.
kps.d: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice identifies fidgeting, increased limb movement and reduced eye contact as invalid indicators that people nevertheless associate with lying. It reports two 2006 meta-analyses finding that purported deception-detection experts perform no better than nonexperts. The authors acknowledge contrary studies and leave open the possibility of reliable verbal cues; they do not reject every potential signal.

kps.k: Mixed group findings and artificial experimental conditions limit conclusions about courtroom fact-finding.
kps.d: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice reports a 2015 study in which groups outperformed individuals, alongside evidence that jury-style deliberation may worsen detection. It also questions the generalisability of an experiment that induced mistaken eyewitness identifications through misleading lineup instructions, while acknowledging that the artificial design may serve other research purposes. This latter issue concerns distinguishing accurate from mistaken testimony, not necessarily detecting intentional deception.

kps.k: Practical assessment should separate scientific reliability, comparative performance and legal admissibility.
kps.d: Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward notes that physiological measures vary in reliability and often interrelate. Its case bibliography documents judicial consideration of admissibility, not judicial acceptance or rejection. Taken together, the sources support scrutinising claims for both human and instrument-based credibility assessment rather than assuming that professional experience, physical presence, a substantial literature or courtroom consideration establishes accuracy. The supplied material does not establish that remote testimony or automated detection improves fact-finding.

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources support the proposition that traditional credibility assessment—especially demeanor-based lie detection and confidence in cross-examination—lacks a secure evidentiary foundation, while no superior technological replacement has been established. Their common reason is methodological caution: apparent expertise, face-to-face observation, the existence of a research literature, and judicial consideration do not themselves demonstrate accuracy. There is material variation in emphasis. Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice provides the stronger empirical challenge, citing poor human deception detection, invalid nonverbal cues and no demonstrated expert advantage, while acknowledging occasional contrary studies, possible verbal cues, conflicting findings about groups and limits arising from artificial experiments. Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward instead contrasts the scientific literature on psychometric methods with largely laudatory treatment of cross-examination, but does not establish comparative superiority; it also stresses variable reliability among physiological measures and distinguishes their scientific reliability from legal admissibility. Thus, these curated sources converge on scrutiny of both human and instrument-based assessment rather than endorsement of either as dependable.

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the proposition by challenging the evidentiary basis of cross-examination while not claiming that psychometric or physiological deception detection is a proven superior replacement. Its reasoning is two-sided but directionally consistent: traditional credibility assessment lacks a comparable scientific literature, yet technological measures differ in reliability and may be interrelated. It also treats judicial consideration of admissibility as distinct from proof of reliability or comparative performance. Internal variation therefore concerns the strength of the technological alternative, not the core critique of conventional assessment. Because this period contains one curated source, no broader prevalence or group consensus can be inferred.

elens.an: Within this curated source evidence for 2023–2024, Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice supports the proposition that demeanor-based credibility assessment is unreliable without establishing a superior technological replacement. Its principal reasons are that humans generally perform poorly at detecting deception across communication media, commonly rely on invalid nonverbal cues, and gain no demonstrated advantage from relevant professional experience. The source also contains material internal variation, but not enough to make its position mixed: it acknowledges occasional contrary studies and the possibility that some verbal cues may be reliable; reports both improved group performance in one study and potentially worse results from jury-style deliberation; and cautions that experimental success in distinguishing accurate from mistaken testimony may depend on artificial conditions. These qualifications reinforce the need for cautious, context-specific assessment rather than restoring confidence in demeanor. The source does not comparatively validate technological lie detection or directly develop the synthesis’s distinction among scientific reliability, comparative performance and legal admissibility, so its position is Supports rather than Builds on.
